paper.title: The importance of workplace accommodation for cancer survivors – The role of flexible work schedules and psychological help in returning to work
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project number are given. …

registers.years: 2004-2011 (employment is observed each year before and after diagnoses made in 2006-2008)
registers.role: outcome, sample frame, controls and linkage
variables_mentioned: age at the end of the diagnosis year
employment each year before and after diagnosis

registers.name_in_paper: hospitalization diagnoses used to build the Charlson comorbidity index
registers.years: 1-10 years prior to the year of cancer diagnosis
variables_mentioned: Charlson comorbidity index 10-1 years before diagnosis

registers.name_in_paper: survey conducted in 2010 on a sample of Danish cancer survivors (fall 2010)
variables_mentioned: ability to work during treatment and one year after treatment (Work Ability Index item)
pre-cancer job dissatisfaction with physical demands

linkages: Survey answers linked to administrative data through a unique link between questionnaire serial numbers and personal identification numbers (p. 2).

sample.universe: All Danish 30-60-year-olds diagnosed with breast, colon or melanoma skin cancer in 2006-2008, not diagnosed with cancer prior to 2006, employed two years before the year of diagnosis, who survived and lived in Denmark at the time of the survey (fall 2010): 4804 individuals.
sample.unit_of_observation: individual cancer survivor (one cross-sectional observation per survey respondent)
selection_rules: Survey population (breast, colon or melanoma skin cancer, 30-60 years, diagnosed 2006-2008, no cancer before 2006, employed two years before diagnosis, alive and resident in Denmark in fall 2010): 4804
2. Survived three years after diagnosis (and did not emigrate): 4590
4. Answered questions on being offered accommodating job initiatives: 3285 (response rate 71.6% = 3285/4590)
sample.period: cancer diagnoses 2006-2008; survey fall 2010; employment outcome in the third year after diagnosis
sample.n_observations: 3285 (2021/1264 by job seniority; 2066/1219 by work experience; 244/3041 by pre-cancer dissatisfaction with the superior; 3247 in the IPW analysis)

construction_notes: Outcome: indicator for being employed in the third year after the diagnosis year; mean 0.866 (SD 0.341) among the 3285 respondents versus 0.686 among the 1305 non-respondents (Table 2, p. 3).

Ability to work is the first item of the Work Ability Index, scored 0 (lowest) to 10 (highest) relative to the respondent's own best; 'after diagnosis' is the average of ability to work during cancer treatment and one year after treatment (Table 2, note c).
Ability to work is entered as three indicators to relax the linear parametrization: low (levels 0-3), medium (levels 4-8), high (levels 9-10), with low omitted.

Change in ability to work = ability after diagnosis minus ability before diagnosis, grouped as high decrease (<= −5, 36.7%, N = 1206), medium decrease (> −5, <= −2.5, 28.4%, N = 932) and low decrease or increase (> −2.5, 30.2%, N = 992), with a missing-change indicator (4.7%, N = 155).

Missing answers on survey-based variables are kept in the sample and flagged with missing-value indicators (flexible schedule 1.2% missing; psychological help 13.8%; ability to work after diagnosis 4.4%).
Diagnosis year dummies (2006, 2007, 2008) are included to control for business cycles and possible recall bias from the lag between diagnosis and the 2010 survey.
Charlson comorbidity index built from hospitalization diagnoses 1-10 years before the year of diagnosis (Charlson et al., 1987; Sundararajan et al., 2004).
Standard errors are heteroscedasticity-robust; the models are linear probability models estimated by OLS.

claims.statement: Among Danish cancer survivors employed before diagnosis, being offered a flexible work schedule during and after cancer treatment raises the probability of being employed three years after diagnosis (Table 3, model (1)).

treatment.label: Flexible schedule (being offered a flexible work schedule during and after cancer treatment)

definition.value: Binary survey indicator. In the 2010 survey respondents were asked “Did you have a flexible work arrangement such that you were able to leave work/stay home if you experienced any physical or mental challenges?”, answered “yes” or “no”. 61.9% of respondents were offered a flexible schedule; 1.2% of answers are missing and a missing-value indicator enters the models.

timing.value: during and after cancer treatment; reported retrospectively in the survey carried out in fall 2010

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark administrative data; the paper does not name the specific register

definition.value: Indicator equal to one if the cancer survivor is employed in the third year after the year of the cancer diagnosis. Built from Statistics Denmark administrative data, which give employment in each year before and after diagnosis. Mean 0.866 (SD 0.341) in the estimation sample of 3285 respondents.

timing.value: third year after the diagnosis year (diagnoses 2006-2008, so employment measured 2009-2011)

units.value: percentage points of the probability of being employed three years after diagnosis (the outcome is a 0/1 indicator; the paper calls them '% points')

magnitude.interpretation: The paper reads the coefficient as the effect of being offered a flexible schedule on the return-to-work probability: 6.6% points.

estimand.target_population: Danish 30-60-year-olds diagnosed with breast, colon or melanoma skin cancer in 2006-2008 who were employed before diagnosis and survived three years; the authors read β₁ as the treatment effect of receiving a flexible schedule for this population.
estimand.time_horizon: employment in the third year after the cancer diagnosis
estimand.formal_query: E[Employed_3y | do(flexible schedule = 1)] - E[Employed_3y | do(flexible schedule = 0)]

population.selection: Survey population: all Danish 30-60-year-olds diagnosed with breast, colon or melanoma skin cancer 2006-2008, not diagnosed with cancer before 2006, employed two years before the diagnosis year, who survived and lived in Denmark in fall 2010 (4804). Restricted to employed the year before diagnosis (4650), surviving three years without emigrating (4590), participating in the survey (3497) and answering the accommodation questions (3285; response rate 71.6%).

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation between cancer survivors in whether the workplace offered a flexible work schedule (and psychological help) during and after cancer treatment, as reported in a 2010 survey linked to Danish administrative data. No reform, instrument, discontinuity or before/after comparison is used; identification rests on controlling for a large set of register- and survey-based covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unconfoundedness given the observed covariates: conditional on the register- and survey-based control variables, being offered a flexible schedule (or psychological help) is independent of potential employment outcomes three years after diagnosis.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue the assumption 'may not be unreasonable' given a very large covariate set (demography, health, job dissatisfaction, ability to work, labour-market attachment); they also report that the probability of being assigned a flexible schedule shows no clear pattern across ability to work, cancer stage, cancer type, work experience, job seniority or education (Appendix Table A.4), and an IPW covariate-balance test (Imai and Ratkovic, 2014) that cannot reject balance.

key_assumptions.assumption: The authors concede that selection on unobservables into being offered a flexible schedule cannot be ruled out: diagnosed employees may select jobs with a flexible schedule, and employers may accommodate only the employees they wish to retain.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues the sign of such a selection bias is not obvious, and shows the flexible-schedule estimate is stable when the sample is stratified on job seniority (Table 5), work experience (Table 6) and pre-cancer dissatisfaction with the superior (Table 7).

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample is conditioned on having been employed the year before diagnosis, on surviving three years without emigrating, on participating in the survey and on answering the accommodation questions; the authors note this is a concern for external validity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 reports the restriction steps and a 71.6% response rate; Table 2 compares respondents with the 1305 non-respondents and reports significant differences in the outcome and several covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Recall bias in the retrospectively reported accommodation and work-ability measures is assumed to be unimportant because the survey questions about accommodation are very specific.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assertion only; the paper also includes diagnosis-year dummies partly to control for possible recall bias due to the lag between diagnosis (2006-2008) and survey (2010), and compares its retrospective work-ability levels with the prospective measurements in De Boer et al. (2008).

threats_discussed: selection into being offered a flexible schedule, on the employee side (seeking a flexible job) and on the employer side (accommodating only employees the employer wishes to retain)
recall bias in retrospective survey answers about accommodation and ability to work
non-response and selection into the sample of respondents, a concern for external validity
conditioning on desire to work after treatment as a possible 'bad control'
robustness_checks: sequential addition of control sets, models (1)-(5) of Table 3
replacing ability to work after diagnosis with the change in ability to work (Table 4)
stratifying on job seniority (Table 5), general work experience (Table 6) and pre-cancer dissatisfaction with the superior (Table 7)
inverse probability weighting with a logit (and probit) treatment model, ATE and ATT, with a covariate balance test (Table 8)
logit models reported as odds ratios and average marginal effects (Appendix Tables A.8 and A.9)
re-estimating all models excluding the psychological help variable (results available on request)
unresolved_confounders: selection on unobservables into being offered a flexible schedule (employee self-selection into flexible jobs; employers accommodating only employees they want to retain)

definition.value: Binary survey indicator. In the 2010 survey respondents were asked “Did you have a flexible work arrangement such that you were able to leave work/stay home if you experienced any physical or mental challenges?”, answered “yes” or “no”. 61.9% of respondents were offered a flexible schedule; 1.2% of answers are missing and a missing-value indicator enters the models.

timing.value: during and after cancer treatment; reported retrospectively in the survey carried out in fall 2010

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark administrative data; the paper does not name the specific register

definition.value: Indicator equal to one if the cancer survivor is employed in the third year after the year of the cancer diagnosis. Built from Statistics Denmark administrative data, which give employment in each year before and after diagnosis. Mean 0.866 (SD 0.341) in the estimation sample of 3285 respondents.

timing.value: third year after the diagnosis year (diagnoses 2006-2008, so employment measured 2009-2011)

units.value: percentage points of the probability of being employed three years after diagnosis (the outcome is a 0/1 indicator; the paper calls them '% points')

magnitude.interpretation: The paper reads the coefficient as the effect of being offered a flexible schedule on the return-to-work probability: 4.9% points.

estimand.target_population: Danish 30-60-year-olds diagnosed with breast, colon or melanoma skin cancer in 2006-2008 who were employed before diagnosis and survived three years; the authors read β₁ as the treatment effect of receiving a flexible schedule for this population.
estimand.time_horizon: employment in the third year after the cancer diagnosis
estimand.formal_query: E[Employed_3y | do(flexible schedule = 1)] - E[Employed_3y | do(flexible schedule = 0)]

population.description: Danish 30-60-year-olds diagnosed with breast, colon or melanoma skin cancer in 2006-2008, not diagnosed with cancer before 2006, employed two years (and the year) before diagnosis, who survived three years without emigrating, participated in the 2010 survey and answered the questions on accommodating job initiatives (N = 3285).
population.ages: 30-60 years at diagnosis (age measured at the end of the diagnosis year; the sample's age range is 30-61, mean 50.235)
population.period: cancer diagnoses 2006-2008; survey carried out in fall 2010; employment outcome measured in the third year after diagnosis
subgroups_defined: ability to work after diagnosis (low 0-3 / medium 4-8 / high 9-10)
ability to work before diagnosis (Appendix Table A.2)
change in ability to work from before to after diagnosis (Appendix Table A.3)
job type (manual or service jobs / other jobs)
level of education (compulsory / vocational / further / higher)
cancer type (colon / melanoma skin / breast)
job seniority (same employer in the four years before diagnosis or not)
general work experience (more than 20 years in the labor market or not)
pre-cancer dissatisfaction with the superior (dissatisfied / not dissatisfied)
population.selection: Survey population: all Danish 30-60-year-olds diagnosed with breast, colon or melanoma skin cancer 2006-2008, not diagnosed with cancer before 2006, employed two years before the diagnosis year, who survived and lived in Denmark in fall 2010 (4804). Restricted to employed the year before diagnosis (4650), surviving three years without emigrating (4590), participating in the survey (3497) and answering the accommodation questions (3285; response rate 71.6%).

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation between cancer survivors in whether the workplace offered a flexible work schedule (and psychological help) during and after cancer treatment, as reported in a 2010 survey linked to Danish administrative data. No reform, instrument, discontinuity or before/after comparison is used; identification rests on controlling for a large set of register- and survey-based covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unconfoundedness given the observed covariates: conditional on the register- and survey-based control variables, being offered a flexible schedule (or psychological help) is independent of potential employment outcomes three years after diagnosis.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue the assumption 'may not be unreasonable' given a very large covariate set (demography, health, job dissatisfaction, ability to work, labour-market attachment); they also report that the probability of being assigned a flexible schedule shows no clear pattern across ability to work, cancer stage, cancer type, work experience, job seniority or education (Appendix Table A.4), and an IPW covariate-balance test (Imai and Ratkovic, 2014) that cannot reject balance.

key_assumptions.assumption: The authors concede that selection on unobservables into being offered a flexible schedule cannot be ruled out: diagnosed employees may select jobs with a flexible schedule, and employers may accommodate only the employees they wish to retain.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues the sign of such a selection bias is not obvious, and shows the flexible-schedule estimate is stable when the sample is stratified on job seniority (Table 5), work experience (Table 6) and pre-cancer dissatisfaction with the superior (Table 7).

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample is conditioned on having been employed the year before diagnosis, on surviving three years without emigrating, on participating in the survey and on answering the accommodation questions; the authors note this is a concern for external validity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 reports the restriction steps and a 71.6% response rate; Table 2 compares respondents with the 1305 non-respondents and reports significant differences in the outcome and several covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Recall bias in the retrospectively reported accommodation and work-ability measures is assumed to be unimportant because the survey questions about accommodation are very specific.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assertion only; the paper also includes diagnosis-year dummies partly to control for possible recall bias due to the lag between diagnosis (2006-2008) and survey (2010), and compares its retrospective work-ability levels with the prospective measurements in De Boer et al. (2008).

key_assumptions.assumption: Desire to work after cancer treatment is treated as a 'bad control' that may itself be affected by the accommodation offered, and is therefore left out of the preferred model (4).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Model (5) of Table 3 adds the variable and the flexible-schedule estimate moves only from 4.9% to 4.6% points.

heterogeneity.finding: The effect of a flexible schedule is 14.3% points for survivors with a low ability to work (levels 0-3) and statistically insignificant for survivors with a medium or a high ability to work (p. 5, Fig. 1).
0.062 (significant at the 1% level) in manual or service jobs versus 0.046 (1% level) in other jobs; the paper states the difference is not statistically significant (p. 5, Fig. 2).
0.093 for compulsory, 0.039 for vocational, 0.059 for further and 0.019 (insignificant) for higher education (p. 5, Fig. 2).
0.087 for colon and 0.062 for breast cancer survivors (the paper states these are not statistically different), and -0.004 (insignificant) for melanoma skin cancer survivors (p. 5 and Fig. 3).
0.049 for survivors with the same employer in the four years before diagnosis and 0.047 for the others; the paper states there is no difference (Table 5, pp. 7-8).
0.050 for more than 20 years in the labor market and 0.045 for 20 years or less; the paper states the effect does not differ significantly (Table 6, p. 8).
0.064 (insignificant, N = 244) for dissatisfied employees and 0.049 (1% level) for the others; the paper states the coefficients do not differ noteworthy (Table 7, p. 8).

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation between cancer survivors in whether the workplace offered a flexible work schedule (and psychological help) during and after cancer treatment, as reported in a 2010 survey linked to Danish administrative data. No reform, instrument, discontinuity or before/after comparison is used; identification rests on controlling for a large set of register- and survey-based covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unconfoundedness given the observed covariates: conditional on the register- and survey-based control variables, being offered a flexible schedule (or psychological help) is independent of potential employment outcomes three years after diagnosis.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue the assumption 'may not be unreasonable' given a very large covariate set (demography, health, job dissatisfaction, ability to work, labour-market attachment); they also report that the probability of being assigned a flexible schedule shows no clear pattern across ability to work, cancer stage, cancer type, work experience, job seniority or education (Appendix Table A.4), and an IPW covariate-balance test (Imai and Ratkovic, 2014) that cannot reject balance.

key_assumptions.assumption: The authors concede that selection on unobservables into being offered a flexible schedule cannot be ruled out: diagnosed employees may select jobs with a flexible schedule, and employers may accommodate only the employees they wish to retain.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues the sign of such a selection bias is not obvious, and shows the flexible-schedule estimate is stable when the sample is stratified on job seniority (Table 5), work experience (Table 6) and pre-cancer dissatisfaction with the superior (Table 7).

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample is conditioned on having been employed the year before diagnosis, on surviving three years without emigrating, on participating in the survey and on answering the accommodation questions; the authors note this is a concern for external validity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 reports the restriction steps and a 71.6% response rate; Table 2 compares respondents with the 1305 non-respondents and reports significant differences in the outcome and several covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Recall bias in the retrospectively reported accommodation and work-ability measures is assumed to be unimportant because the survey questions about accommodation are very specific.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assertion only; the paper also includes diagnosis-year dummies partly to control for possible recall bias due to the lag between diagnosis (2006-2008) and survey (2010), and compares its retrospective work-ability levels with the prospective measurements in De Boer et al. key_assumptions.assumption: Unconfoundedness given the observed covariates: conditional on the register- and survey-based control variables, being offered a flexible schedule (or psychological help) is independent of potential employment outcomes three years after diagnosis.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue the assumption 'may not be unreasonable' given a very large covariate set (demography, health, job dissatisfaction, ability to work, labour-market attachment); they also report that the probability of being assigned a flexible schedule shows no clear pattern across ability to work, cancer stage, cancer type, work experience, job seniority or education (Appendix Table A.4), and an IPW covariate-balance test (Imai and Ratkovic, 2014) that cannot reject balance.

key_assumptions.assumption: The authors concede that selection on unobservables into being offered a flexible schedule cannot be ruled out: diagnosed employees may select jobs with a flexible schedule, and employers may accommodate only the employees they wish to retain.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unconfoundedness given the observed covariates: conditional on the register- and survey-based control variables, being offered a flexible schedule (or psychological help) is independent of potential employment outcomes three years after diagnosis.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue the assumption 'may not be unreasonable' given a very large covariate set (demography, health, job dissatisfaction, ability to work, labour-market attachment); they also report that the probability of being assigned a flexible schedule shows no clear pattern across ability to work, cancer stage, cancer type, work experience, job seniority or education (Appendix Table A.4), and an IPW covariate-balance test (Imai and Ratkovic, 2014) that cannot reject balance.

key_assumptions.assumption: The authors concede that selection on unobservables into being offered a flexible schedule cannot be ruled out: diagnosed employees may select jobs with a flexible schedule, and employers may accommodate only the employees they wish to retain.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues the sign of such a selection bias is not obvious, and shows the flexible-schedule estimate is stable when the sample is stratified on job seniority (Table 5), work experience (Table 6) and pre-cancer dissatisfaction with the superior (Table 7).

key_assumptions.assumption: Unconfoundedness given the observed covariates: conditional on the register- and survey-based control variables, being offered a flexible schedule (or psychological help) is independent of potential employment outcomes three years after diagnosis.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue the assumption 'may not be unreasonable' given a very large covariate set (demography, health, job dissatisfaction, ability to work, labour-market attachment); they also report that the probability of being assigned a flexible schedule shows no clear pattern across ability to work, cancer stage, cancer type, work experience, job seniority or education (Appendix Table A.4), and an IPW covariate-balance test (Imai and Ratkovic, 2014) that cannot reject balance.

key_assumptions.assumption: The authors concede that selection on unobservables into being offered a flexible schedule cannot be ruled out: diagnosed employees may select jobs with a flexible schedule, and employers may accommodate only the employees they wish to retain.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues the sign of such a selection bias is not obvious, and shows the flexible-schedule estimate is stable when the sample is stratified on job seniority (Table 5), work experience (Table 6) and pre-cancer dissatisfaction with the superior (Table 7).

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample is conditioned on having been employed the year before diagnosis, on surviving three years without emigrating, on participating in the survey and on answering the accommodation questions; the authors note this is a concern for external validity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 reports the restriction steps and a 71.6% response rate; Table 2 compares respondents with the 1305 non-respondents and reports significant differences in the outcome and several covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Recall bias in the retrospectively reported accommodation and work-ability measures is assumed to be unimportant because the survey questions about accommodation are very specific.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assertion only; the paper also includes diagnosis-year dummies partly to control for possible recall bias due to the lag between diagnosis (2006-2008) and survey (2010), and compares its retrospective work-ability levels with the prospective measurements in De Boer et al. key_assumptions.supported_by: Model (5) of Table 3 adds the variable and the flexible-schedule estimate moves only from 4.9% to 4.6% points.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unconfoundedness given the observed covariates: conditional on the register- and survey-based control variables, being offered a flexible schedule (or psychological help) is independent of potential employment outcomes three years after diagnosis.

key_assumptions.assumption: The authors concede that selection on unobservables into being offered a flexible schedule cannot be ruled out: diagnosed employees may select jobs with a flexible schedule, and employers may accommodate only the employees they wish to retain.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues the sign of such a selection bias is not obvious, and shows the flexible-schedule estimate is stable when the sample is stratified on job seniority (Table 5), work experience (Table 6) and pre-cancer dissatisfaction with the superior (Table 7).

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample is conditioned on having been employed the year before diagnosis, on surviving three years without emigrating, on participating in the survey and on answering the accommodation questions; the authors note this is a concern for external validity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 reports the restriction steps and a 71.6% response rate; Table 2 compares respondents with the 1305 non-respondents and reports significant differences in the outcome and several covariates.

claims.statement: Being offered psychological help by the workplace has no significant effect on the probability of being employed three years after diagnosis among cancer survivors with high ability to work after diagnosis (levels 9-10; 19.5% of respondents) (Fig. 1).

treatment.label: Psychologist in firm (being offered counselling with a psychologist/personal mentor by the workplace)

definition.value: Binary survey indicator. Respondents were asked whether they were offered counselling with a psychologist/personal mentor during treatment and/or when they returned to work; if yes, who offered it (“My workplace”, “The hospital”, “Other”). The variable records counselling offered by the workplace. 6.1% were offered psychological help by the workplace; 13.8% of answers are missing and a missing-value indicator enters the models.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation between cancer survivors in whether the workplace offered a flexible work schedule (and psychological help) during and after cancer treatment, as reported in a 2010 survey linked to Danish administrative data. No reform, instrument, discontinuity or before/after comparison is used; identification rests on controlling for a large set of register- and survey-based covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unconfoundedness given the observed covariates: conditional on the register- and survey-based control variables, being offered a flexible schedule (or psychological help) is independent of potential employment outcomes three years after diagnosis.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue the assumption 'may not be unreasonable' given a very large covariate set (demography, health, job dissatisfaction, ability to work, labour-market attachment); they also report that the probability of being assigned a flexible schedule shows no clear pattern across ability to work, cancer stage, cancer type, work experience, job seniority or education (Appendix Table A.4), and an IPW covariate-balance test (Imai and Ratkovic, 2014) that cannot reject balance.

key_assumptions.assumption: The authors concede that selection on unobservables into being offered a flexible schedule cannot be ruled out: diagnosed employees may select jobs with a flexible schedule, and employers may accommodate only the employees they wish to retain.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues the sign of such a selection bias is not obvious, and shows the flexible-schedule estimate is stable when the sample is stratified on job seniority (Table 5), work experience (Table 6) and pre-cancer dissatisfaction with the superior (Table 7).

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample is conditioned on having been employed the year before diagnosis, on surviving three years without emigrating, on participating in the survey and on answering the accommodation questions; the authors note this is a concern for external validity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 reports the restriction steps and a 71.6% response rate; Table 2 compares respondents with the 1305 non-respondents and reports significant differences in the outcome and several covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Recall bias in the retrospectively reported accommodation and work-ability measures is assumed to be unimportant because the survey questions about accommodation are very specific.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assertion only; the paper also includes diagnosis-year dummies partly to control for possible recall bias due to the lag between diagnosis (2006-2008) and survey (2010), and compares its retrospective work-ability levels with the prospective measurements in De Boer et al. (2008).

key_assumptions.assumption: Desire to work after cancer treatment is treated as a 'bad control' that may itself be affected by the accommodation offered, and is therefore left out of the preferred model (4).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Model (5) of Table 3 adds the variable and the flexible-schedule estimate moves only from 4.9% to 4.6% points.

Restricted to employed the year before diagnosis (4650), surviving three years without emigrating (4590), participating in the survey (3497) and answering the accommodation questions (3285; response rate 71.6%).

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation between cancer survivors in whether the workplace offered a flexible work schedule (and psychological help) during and after cancer treatment, as reported in a 2010 survey linked to Danish administrative data. No reform, instrument, discontinuity or before/after comparison is used; identification rests on controlling for a large set of register- and survey-based covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Unconfoundedness given the observed covariates: conditional on the register- and survey-based control variables, being offered a flexible schedule (or psychological help) is independent of potential employment outcomes three years after diagnosis.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue the assumption 'may not be unreasonable' given a very large covariate set (demography, health, job dissatisfaction, ability to work, labour-market attachment); they also report that the probability of being assigned a flexible schedule shows no clear pattern across ability to work, cancer stage, cancer type, work experience, job seniority or education (Appendix Table A.4), and an IPW covariate-balance test (Imai and Ratkovic, 2014) that cannot reject balance.

key_assumptions.assumption: The authors concede that selection on unobservables into being offered a flexible schedule cannot be ruled out: diagnosed employees may select jobs with a flexible schedule, and employers may accommodate only the employees they wish to retain.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues the sign of such a selection bias is not obvious, and shows the flexible-schedule estimate is stable when the sample is stratified on job seniority (Table 5), work experience (Table 6) and pre-cancer dissatisfaction with the superior (Table 7).

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample is conditioned on having been employed the year before diagnosis, on surviving three years without emigrating, on participating in the survey and on answering the accommodation questions; the authors note this is a concern for external validity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 reports the restriction steps and a 71.6% response rate; Table 2 compares respondents with the 1305 non-respondents and reports significant differences in the outcome and several covariates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Recall bias in the retrospectively reported accommodation and work-ability measures is assumed to be unimportant because the survey questions about accommodation are very specific.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Assertion only; the paper also includes diagnosis-year dummies partly to control for possible recall bias due to the lag between diagnosis (2006-2008) and survey (2010), and compares its retrospective work-ability levels with the prospective measurements in De Boer et al. (2008).

key_assumptions.assumption: Desire to work after cancer treatment is treated as a 'bad control' that may itself be affected by the accommodation offered, and is therefore left out of the preferred model (4).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Model (5) of Table 3 adds the variable and the flexible-schedule estimate moves only from 4.9% to 4.6% points.
